intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the ASCC1 gene, which encodes a subunit of the activating signal cointegrator 1 (ASC-1) complex.

paragraphs.text: Spinal muscular atrophy with congenital bone fractures-2 (SMABF2) is a rare autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder characterized by arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and prenatal fractures of the long bones, with poor prognosis (Giuffrida et al., 2020). Affected individuals present with prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, respiratory distress, and congenital bone fractures (Knierim et al., 2016; Bohm et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: Bohm et al. (2019) provided clinical, histologic, and genetic descriptions of 3 additional families. All patients had severe prenatal-onset muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis, and congenital bone fractures. Muscle biopsies from the affected infants showed intense oxidative rims beneath the sarcolemma and scattered remnants of sarcomeres with enlarged Z-bands, which the authors suggested might be a histopathologic hallmark of the disorder.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. (2016) used autozygosity mapping and whole-exome sequencing in 4 families with prenatal-onset spinal muscular atrophy and congenital bone fractures. They identified homozygous and compound heterozygous nonsense and frameshift mutations in the TRIP4 and ASCC1 genes, which encode subunits of the nuclear ASC-1 complex. The mutations caused truncation or complete absence of the respective proteins and cosegregated with the disease. ASCC1-mutant fibroblasts showed downregulation of genes associated with neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and pathfinding (SERPINF1, DAB1, SEMA3D, SEMA3A) and with bone development (TNFRSF11B, RASSF2, STC1). Immunoprecipitation of the ASC-1 complex consistently copurified the transcriptional cofactor CSRP1.

paragraphs.text: In a female newborn with SMABF2, Oliveira et al. (2017) used whole-exome sequencing and found a homozygous 1-bp duplication in the ASCC1 gene (c.157dupG), resulting in a frameshift (Glu53GlyfsTer19). Filtering of genes associated with congenital myopathies, muscle diseases, and other neuromuscular disorders had not identified a disease-causing variant. The authors described this as the second known case of ASCC1 involvement.

paragraphs.text: In a stillbirth with SMABF2, Giuffrida et al. (2020) found compound heterozygous mutations in the ASCC1 gene. Microarray analysis first detected a deletion copy number variant of about 64 kb that involved 4 exons of ASCC1. Exome analysis then identified a nonsense mutation (c.1027C-T; Arg343Ter) on the other allele. The authors described this as the first case of ASCC1 compound heterozygosity involving an exonic microdeletion and a nucleotide variant.

paragraphs.text: Knierim et al. agent.process_note: All 4 papers are available only as abstracts, and I read each one in full. The abstract of Knierim et al. (2016) does not name the specific ASCC1 mutation or say how families were split between TRIP4 and ASCC1, so I took the 3 TRIP4 / 1 ASCC1 split from Oliveira et al. (2017). The abstract of Bohm et al. (2019) does not name its 2 novel mutations. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I left out the ASCC1 MIM number and its chromosomal location.
